answer.exemplar: The principle is a claim about legitimate authority, and the difficulty is that the people who are supposed to exercise it are not defined by anything the principle itself supplies. A count gives a distribution rather than a unit, so a group that is a minority across a whole state can be a decisive majority in one district and almost absent from the next, and there is no rule in the principle for choosing between them. The second problem is that peoples are mixed, so any line drawn to satisfy one group places members of others on the wrong side, and those members are themselves entitled to a claim, which is how a single partition generates several further claims. The third is that self-determination is invoked at a moment of weakness, when a state's authority has already broken down, so a decision taken then is made without a functioning authority to record or enforce it. Finally, the principle is used by states as well as by peoples, which makes a neighbouring state with a large population across the border a claimant in its own right. The honest conclusion is not that the principle is empty but that its application is a political judgement about communities and units that the principle constrains without determining.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to identify the source of the difficulty rather than describe the conflict it produces. It lies in the gap between what the principle says and what a count supplies. A principle about who ought to choose their political unit does not tell you which people count, at what level of aggregation they count, or what unit is acceptable, and each of those is a political judgement that the principle constrains without settling. The mixing of populations is the second source, and it is the one that makes partition self-propagating, because a group left on the wrong side of a line has a claim of its own. The timing of the claim is the third, since a claim arrives when the authority it disputes has already weakened. The tempting explanation is that the principle is vague, but vagueness is not the problem in itself: a principle can be clear and still leave these four questions open.
questions.hint: Ask what a census actually supplies against what the principle asks for.

questions.explanation: The tests run in the order the convention sets out. First the risk has to be established, because everything else is conditional on there being a risk to protect against. Second, the risk has to be one the state cannot control, since a state that could stop the harm is expected to do so and the person can then be dealt with by its own authorities. Third, the person has to be unable to escape the risk by moving elsewhere inside their own country, which is the test of internal relocation and the one most often overlooked. Only then is the finding recorded, together with the protection or the refusal that follows from it. The sequence is worth learning as a sequence because the order is substantive: applying the relocation test first, as the second option would, lets a government defeat a claim by pointing to a place the person has never been able to reach.

questions.explanation: Effective protection is netted against the value added at home, not against the whole price. Take a finished good worth 100, of which 60 is imported input and 40 is domestic value added. The error to divide by 100 is to report the 19 as a percentage of the final price, which gives 19 percent and flatters the scheme, because it measures protection against the whole good rather than against the part produced at home.

questions.explanation: A currency union removes two instruments together, and they are usually named separately to make the point clearer. The first is the interest rate, which is now set for the group as a whole by a single authority, so a member cannot lower rates to support its own economy in a downturn. The second is the exchange rate, which can no longer be moved to cushion a shock, so a member that loses export price has no currency lever to pull and must take the adjustment in wages, prices and output instead. The gain is the other side of the same coin, since a common currency removes the risk of a sudden devaluation between members and cuts the cost of trade and borrowing among them. The remaining options are not consequences a currency union produces: notes, tariffs and defence budgets all stay where they were.

answer.exemplar: The argument is that the rimland is where the two great approaches to power meet, and that its value comes from being contested rather than from its size. A coastal fringe is where seaborne trade arrives, where the harbours and the industrial belt around them are, and where any state that wants to reach the interior has to pass or be prevented from passing. It is also where most of the population and most of the economic activity are concentrated, so an army that reaches it has not won a position but has arrived where the wealth is. A sea power and a land power meet there, and the friction between them is generated rather than inherited, which is why the theory treats the margin as the decisive zone rather than as a border. The claim is a claim about leverage rather than about territory: a state holding the rimland can choose to open or close the routes through it, and can tax the traffic that crosses. The counter-argument is that the idea concentrates attention on coastlines and can neglect inland economies, and that technology can carry a route past a contested shore altogether.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to make clear that the case is about leverage and not about area, and that the leverage comes from the meeting of two systems of movement. A fringe between the sea and the interior is where cargoes change hands, where a naval power can be obstructed, and where the population and capital of a continent are usually concentrated, so control of it is control of the profitable part rather than of the empty part. The generating role matters as much as the geography, because the friction between a sea power and a land power is produced where their routes cross, and a theory built on that crossing will treat the zone as permanently contested. The explanation is incomplete without acknowledging the objection, which is that a coastline can be bypassed and that a fixated idea of the margin neglects inland economies entirely, which is why the later versions of this argument treat the rim as a band rather than a line.

answer.exemplar: The claim is a chain of conditionals and each link is contestable. The first objection is historical: the theory was built on the pattern of land power in one period, when artillery and railways rewarded interior lines, and the same period did not produce the dominance it predicts, since the industrial and maritime powers of that era were not the states holding the heartland. The second is technological, because sea power and long-range air power let an outside power reach and supply an interior without holding the ground between, so the condition the theory relies on can be bypassed rather than obeyed. The third is that the resource list is not stable, since the things that make an interior valuable change with technology, and a region rich in one era is ordinary in the next. The fourth is that the theory is indeterminate, because it explains whatever happens after the event, since a state that fails to dominate can be said to have held the wrong interior. None of these settles the question, and the honest conclusion is that interior position raises the cost of projecting power rather than guaranteeing it.

questions.explanation: The objections have to be given as a set, because they attack different links in the same chain. The historical one is the plainest: the theory was formulated from a period whose land power came from the interior, and the states that actually dominated in that period were not the ones the theory would have chosen. The technological one matters more now, because sea and air power compress distance, so the cost of reaching a distant interior falls without anyone taking the ground in between, and a precondition that can be circumvented is not a precondition. The instability of the resource list is a third, since what makes an interior worth holding is a function of the technology of the day. The indeterminacy objection is the most damaging, because a theory that explains every outcome has stopped being tested by any of them. What survives all of this is a weaker proposition, that interior depth reduces the cost of sustained projection.

answer.exemplar: The revenue arrives, but whether it becomes income for the country depends on institutions that have to do several things at once. A resource is a rent, meaning a payment for the use of something the country owns, and rent does not automatically become income, because it can be captured by whoever controls the route, the price and the licence. The classic mechanisms of failure are four. The state may tax the revenue so heavily that the firms move elsewhere, losing the activity and the tax together. The currency may appreciate, which makes the rest of the country's exports uncompetitive, so one booming sector hollows out the others. The whole economy may come to depend on one price, and one price fall then damages the budget, the currency and the banks at the same time. And the revenue may be spent on imported goods and on rents for supporters rather than on anything that raises the country's own productivity, so that nothing is left behind when the rent falls. Whether the curse appears therefore turns on whether the state can save, invest and stabilise, and there is nothing automatic about any of that.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to show that the resource and the outcome are connected only through institutions, and then name the channels rather than leaving them as a list. A rent is a payment for owning something scarce, and it is not the same as income, because it goes to whoever can capture it, and the capture can happen through taxation, through ownership of the route, or through who sets the price. From that, four mechanisms follow, and each is a way of losing the gain rather than of failing to obtain it. Over-taxation drives the activity elsewhere. Appreciation damages every other export. Concentration in one commodity makes the whole budget and the currency exposed to one price. And spending the revenue on consumption and on political patronage leaves nothing behind to be earned when the rent falls. What decides the outcome is therefore whether the state can save part of the windfall, invest it in productivity, and stabilise the currency, none of which follows from finding the deposit.

answer.exemplar: A veto turns a majority rule into a rule about unanimity among a small group, because a single holder of the blocking right can stop anything the rest agree on. Two things follow. The first is on decisions: the institution can only act where the interests of the veto holders and the interests of the majority overlap, so the agenda shrinks towards what those states will accept, and matters they do not care about become the ones that get done, often by default. The second is on bargaining: because a veto holder knows that a bare majority is not enough, the others have to bring it something, so the institution works by bargaining packages rather than by voting, and a small state that holds no veto is most often the party that pays for a deal struck by larger ones. The holders are not merely protected but privileged, because their immunity from enforcement lets them extract concessions that others, unable to threaten a veto, cannot. That is why the argument about reforming such a body is usually an argument about who may block, and why an institution dominated by veto holders can be busy and yet settle very little.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to show the effect on two different parties, because the veto does different things to the body and to those outside it. On the body, a blocking right converts a majority decision into a negotiated one, since no measure survives without the consent of the holders, and the practical consequence is an agenda that has been trimmed to what those states will accept. On the rest of the membership, the veto is a source of bargaining power that can be used precisely because it is credible, so a holder can trade a threat to block for concessions on something else, and the payments come from members who cannot offer the same threat. The argument is incomplete without saying who is not in the room, since a small member that pays for deals reached among large ones has a reason to object to the arrangement quite apart from any principle. What is not implied is paralysis: a body with a veto can be extremely active where the holders agree.
questions.hint: Ask what a majority can no longer do on its own, and who benefits from that.

The error to avoid is dividing 96,000 by 6 and getting 16,000, which mixes people with litres, and reporting the daily litres of 576,000 as though it were a count of containers.

answer.exemplar: The protection that follows a border crossing is not attached to the crossing, which is why two people can cross at the same post on the same morning and go out through different doors. What decides the category is a set of tests applied to the person, not to the act. One person has a well-founded fear of serious harm on a protected ground, and their own state cannot control that harm and cannot remove it by letting them move elsewhere inside the country, and that finding brings the prohibition on being returned to the place of the fear. The other left for a job, or to join a family, and intends to return, and none of the tests applies to them, so they are free to enter and to leave on the ordinary terms that apply to any foreign national, which may include a work permit and may include being required to leave. This is why a count of people crossing a border is not a count of refugees, and why the same person can be recognised on one crossing and recognised again on the next. It also explains why the tests are applied individually, since a large number of clearly economic crossings tells an officer nothing about the case in front of them.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to separate the act from the status, since the whole item turns on that separation, and then name the tests that do the separating. Protection follows a finding about a person: a well-founded fear of serious harm, a state unable to control it, and no safe place inside that state. Ordinary movement is what remains when none of those tests is met, and it is governed by the ordinary rules on entry, work and return that apply to foreign nationals in general. The reason this matters practically is that the two categories are counted differently and carry different consequences, so a total of people crossing a border cannot be read as a total of refugees, and a claim of a large refugee movement can look large simply because a large seasonal labour flow has been included. The explanation is incomplete without noting that the tests are applied person by person, since nothing about the movement itself settles them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the tests apply to the crossing or to the person who made it.
questions.learningObjective: explain why the same border crossing carries different statuses

questions.explanation: A claim to act alone has to be tested against the rule that would prevent it, and the rule has two parts that can be examined separately. The first is whether the matter falls within the body's remit, because a body with no jurisdiction over a matter cannot block it, and a state that can show the subject falls outside is on strong ground. The second is who may block, because a council in which a handful of states can stop any decision gives a small state a reason to press the first point rather than to expect a majority. Together these make the claim assessable against a document, which is what the other options are not. Reserves are a question of capacity, a seat is a question about the membership rule rather than the claim, and asking who would win is a question about the outcome of a vote the state says should not be held at all.

questions.explanation: The assessment runs from the geography outwards. The narrowings have to be found first, because what makes a route matter is a single point through which an unusual share of traffic must pass, and a route without a narrowing is not a chokepoint whatever its tonnage. The share of trade is measured next, since a narrowing carrying a twentieth of the traffic is a different proposition from one carrying a half, and the number is also needed before any cost can be attributed to closing it. The detour follows, because the size of the extra distance and time is what converts a traffic share into an economic loss, and it is only meaningful once the share is known. The alternatives come last, since they determine how much of the loss is actually borne and what the traffic would do instead. Reversing the first two steps produces a figure that looks impressive and means nothing.
questions.hint: Find the narrowing first, then measure the traffic, then cost the detour, then the alternatives.
